**Lab pack:** [lab04.tar.gz](../labs/lab04.tar.gz) — pre-placed on lab machines, downloadable for home practice.

**Syllabus practical modules:** 5 and 6 — `for` loops, and `while` / `do-while` loops.
They are taught together on purpose: the three forms are one idea in three costumes, and
converting between them is a better exercise than meeting them a week apart.

**Evaluation:** Graded — equal weight within the 20% lab component. Ten drills, five
fill-in-the-blank programs, and three checked problems, plus observed work and a short
viva. Teams of 1–2; pairs swap driver/navigator at half-time.

**Lab manual:** [The C Programming Laboratory](../labs/CLab3_Aroof.pdf) — the department's shared reference (vim §1 · the compilation model §2.5 · types and `#define` §2.7–2.8 · the operator precedence table §2.9–2.10 · `printf`/`scanf` §3). This sheet is self-contained; the manual is there when you want more.

## What changes today

**You write the `scanf` now.** Until last week the reading was done for you and you
supplied the thinking. From today the starters give you the declarations and the final
`printf` — nothing else. The scaffolding comes away one plank at a time; this is the
first plank.

**And the starters do not compile as shipped.** That is deliberate. Every blank is a
name the compiler has never heard of, so instead of a wrong answer you get a message
naming the exact line still waiting for you:

```
e3.c:19:5: error: use of undeclared identifier 'TODO_read_a_and_b'
```

## Act 1 · Drills — predict, then run (25 min)

Ten drills. For each: **see it, write down what you think happens, and only then run it.**

```bash
./drill.sh --all
```

| Drills | Territory |
|---|---|
| `t01` | one type conversion, to keep it warm — does a `float` variable rescue an `int` division? |
| `p01`–`p04` | precedence, aimed straight at **loop conditions**: a comparison is a *value*; `0 < n < 3` lies; `<` vs `<=` at the boundary; and `=` is not `==` |
| `L1`–`L5` | **the compiler pipeline, by hand** — the four stages from Monday's lecture, one command each, ending at `nm` and the `U printf` that explains why linkers exist |

A wrong prediction scores exactly as much as a right one — but only if you write it down
first. `L1`–`L5` are self-marked; marking yourself right when you were not simply throws
away the one record that shows you what to revise.

## Act 2 · Fill the blanks (25 min)

Five programs, each missing its `scanf` and the lines that make the loop move.

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `b1_sum_while.c` | add 1 + 2 + … + n, with a `while` |
| `b2_sum_for.c` | **the same sum, as a `for`** — convert it; do not copy it |
| `b3_digits.c` | how many digits does n have? (`/10` until it runs out) |
| `b4_factorial.c` | n! — and the GIVEN stops at 12. Work out why |
| `b5_digits0.c` | digits again, but n may be **0** |

::: {.callout-tip}
Do `b3` first, then feed your answer `0`. It says **zero digits** — wrong, because a
`while` checks *before* it runs, so the body never runs at all. `b5` is the same problem
with `do-while`, which checks *after*. That contrast is the entire reason C has three
loops instead of one.
:::

## Act 3 · The checked three (40 min, solo)

| Problem | Task | Final line ends with exactly |
|---|---|---|
| `e1.c` | sum and count of the even numbers up to n | `sum=<S> count=<C>` |
| `e2.c` | reverse the digits of n | `rev=<R>` |
| `e3.c` | greatest common divisor of two numbers | `gcd=<G>` |

`e2` has a public example worth reading twice: `900` → `rev=9`. Reversed, 900 is 009, and
a number has no leading zeros. The checker *will* draw numbers ending in zero.

`e3` is Euclid, 300 BC. The whole algorithm rests on one fact — **`gcd(a, b)` is the same
number as `gcd(b, a % b)`**. Check it by hand on 48 and 18 before you write anything. The
pair keeps changing; the answer never does. That unchanging thing is a **loop invariant**,
and it is why you may stop the moment `b` reaches 0.

**How checking works** — as before: `./check.sh e1` compiles *your source* and runs it on
the public examples **and on fresh random inputs drawn from the GIVEN**. A program that
memorises an example fails the next draw. New this week: if the checker says **`TIMEOUT`**,
your loop never ends — nothing is wrong with the machine.

## Act 4 · Check, fix, bundle (10 min)

```bash
./check.sh
```

Fix, re-check, repeat. Then — green or time-up (an imperfect bundle beats no bundle):

```bash
./check.sh --bundle
```

Carry `../lab04_<rolls>_<branch>_w<NN>.tar.gz` out with you (Moodle + email yourself).
The machine forgets.

## Stretch (fast finishers)

- **The triangle, properly.** Lab 02's stretch made you print a 4-row triangle with *one
  `printf` per line*, because you had no loops. Write it again with nested loops, and make
  the number of rows something the user types. Then read the two versions side by side —
  that diff is three weeks of progress.
- **Convert all three.** Rewrite `e1` as a `while`, `e2` as a `for`, `e3` as a `do-while`.
  One of the three will fight you. Which, and why?
- **Count the rounds.** Add a counter to `e3` and print how many times the loop ran for
  `48 18`, then for two large numbers close together. Euclid is fast — how fast?
